_meta.note: Hand-authored British and Irish catalog: London, Liverpool, Manchester, Birmingham, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Leeds, Newcastle, Cardiff, Belfast and Dublin. Shaped like Qloo Insights entities plus a `_syn` block used for scoring and stripped before serving. Entity ids are fake. Not Qloo data.

properties.short_description: The Liverpool four who changed popular music between 1962 and 1970: 'She Loves You', 'Yesterday', 'Hey Jude'.
'Living Doll', 'Summer Holiday', 'The Young Ones': Britain's first rock-and-roll star, with The Shadows behind him.
'Apache' (1960), 'Wonderful Land', the twanging Stratocaster and the Shadows walk.
The Forces' Sweetheart: 'We'll Meet Again', 'The White Cliffs of Dover', the voice of the war years and after.
'(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction', 'Paint It Black', 'Brown Sugar': the other band of the sixties, from Dartford and Richmond.
'I Only Want to Be with You', 'You Don't Have to Say You Love Me', 'Son of a Preacher Man'; the beehive and the blue-eyed soul.
'It's Not Unusual' (1965), 'Delilah', 'Green, Green Grass of Home': the voice from Pontypridd.
'Goldfinger', 'Diamonds Are Forever', 'Big Spender': the Tiger Bay girl who became the Bond voice.
'You Really Got Me', 'Waterloo Sunset', 'Lola': Muswell Hill's own, Ray and Dave Davies.
'Downtown' (1964), 'Don't Sleep in the Subway', 'I Know a Place': the child star who conquered the sixties.
'Anyone Who Had a Heart', 'You're My World': the Cavern cloakroom girl who became a national fixture.
'Ferry Cross the Mersey', 'You'll Never Walk Alone': Merseybeat's second band, the Kop's anthem.
'Bus Stop', 'He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother', 'The Air That I Breathe': Manchester harmonies.
'I'm into Something Good', 'Mrs. Brown, You've Got a Lovely Daughter': Peter Noone and the Manchester boys next door.
'Shout' (1964), 'To Sir with Love', 'Boom Bang-a-Bang': the Glasgow girl with the big voice.
'Release Me' (1967), 'The Last Waltz': the ballads that kept the Beatles off number one.
'Portrait of My Love', 'From Russia with Love', 'Born Free': the singing bus driver from Shoreditch.
'My Generation', 'Pinball Wizard', 'Won't Get Fooled Again': Shepherd's Bush mods, the loudest band in the world.
'You Need Hands', 'Tulips from Amsterdam', the Singalongamax albums and the family sing-song.
'Rock Island Line' (1956), 'My Old Man's a Dustman': the king of skiffle, with a washboard and a tea chest.
'Scotland the Brave', 'The Song of the Clyde': the tenor of a thousand Hogmanays.
'Seven Drunken Nights', 'The Wild Rover', 'Whiskey in the Jar': the beards and the ballads from O'Donoghue's.
The Aran sweaters on the Ed Sullivan Show: 'The Jug of Punch', 'The Irish Rover', with Tommy Makem.

properties.short_description: 'Brown Eyed Girl' (1967), 'Moondance', Astral Weeks: Belfast's own, from Them onward.

properties.description: David Lean's desert epic with Peter O'Toole, seven Oscars.
The Beatles' first film, a day in the life of a band on the run from its fans.
Rorke's Drift, 1879, with Stanley Baker and a young Michael Caine; 'Men of Harlech' over the ramparts.
Michael Caine's Cockney Lothario talking straight to the camera; 'What's it all about?'
Minis down the steps of Turin and Caine's 'You're only supposed to blow the bloody doors off!'
Sid James, Barbara Windsor and the bra that pings off in the exercise class; the best-loved of the Carry Ons.
Lionel Bart's musical of the Dickens novel, 'Food, Glorious Food' and 'Consider Yourself'; Best Picture.
Ken Loach's Barnsley boy and his kestrel.
Celia Johnson and Trevor Howard at the station tea room, Rachmaninov in the air.
Alec Guinness's gang of crooks against a little old lady in King's Cross; Ealing's last great comedy.
Two couples and two veteran cars on the London to Brighton run.
Richard Todd as Guy Gibson and the bouncing bomb; the march everyone can hum.
Cliff Richard and The Shadows drive a London double-decker to Athens.
Sean Connery's first Bond, Ursula Andress out of the Jamaican sea.
The Aston Martin, Oddjob's hat, Shirley Bassey's title song.
Albert Finney's Nottingham lathe worker: 'Don't let the bastards grind you down.'
Rita Tushingham in Salford, in the kitchen-sink film of Shelagh Delaney's play.
Tom Courtenay daydreams his way around a Yorkshire town; Julie Christie swings her bag down the street.
Julie Christie as Bathsheba in John Schlesinger's Dorset.
Jenny Agutter waving her petticoat on the Keighley and Worth Valley line; 'Daddy, my Daddy!'
Michael Caine comes home to Newcastle to find out who killed his brother.
An island of Hebrideans and a shipwreck full of whisky; Ealing at its gentlest.
Bill Forsyth's Cumbernauld schoolboy in love with the striker.
John Wayne and Maureen O'Hara in Cong, Technicolor Ireland for the world.
David Lean's Dingle peninsula, Sarah Miles and the storm on the beach.
The Rovers Return, Ena Sharples in the snug, Elsie Tanner: the Weatherfield street since December 1960.
Thursday nights from a Manchester church hall, then the BBC: the chart countdown that every family watched.
William Hartnell, the police box and the Daleks, from behind the sofa.
Captain Mainwaring's Walmington-on-Sea Home Guard: 'Don't panic!' and 'Stupid boy.'
Harold and Albert, rag-and-bone men of Shepherd's Bush; 'You dirty old man.'
Eric and Ernie, the Christmas shows, André Previn and all the right notes.
Panda cars on the Merseyside estates; the police series that put the sixties on screen.
Steed's bowler hat and Emma Peel's catsuit.
'Evening, all.' Jack Warner's beat bobby, every Saturday for twenty-one years.
Hughie Green's talent show and the clapometer; 'I mean that most sincerely, folks.'
Barker and Corbett, 'Four Candles' and the news items at the end.
Grace Brothers' menswear and ladieswear; Mrs Slocombe's hair, Mr Humphries' 'I'm free!'
Sticky-backed plastic, the badge, the tortoise and the elephant that would not behave.
165 Eaton Place, the Bellamys above and Hudson and Mrs Bridges below.
Warren Mitchell's Alf Garnett, ranting from his armchair in Wapping.
Tom and Barbara go self-sufficient in Surbiton; Margo next door is not amused.
Basil, Sybil, Manuel and the Torquay hotel; twelve episodes and all of them perfect.
Bruce Forsyth, 'Didn't he do well?' and the conveyor belt; cuddly toy!
'The weekend starts here!' Cathy McGowan and the mods, live on a Friday.

properties.description: Beat the Clock, the revolving stage and the biggest stars in the world on a Sunday night.
Gay Byrne on RTÉ on a Saturday night, and then a Friday; the longest-running chat show in the world.
RTÉ's flying caravan with Godmother, O'Brien and Judge the dog.
London's oldest restaurant (1798) in Covent Garden: game, pies and puddings.
The Nippies in black and white, tea and a bun at the Coventry Street Corner House; the Corner Houses closed in 1977.
Roast beef carved from the silver trolley, since 1828.
Pie, mash and liquor on Tower Bridge Road since 1902, the oldest pie shop in London.
The Soho espresso bar since 1949, open all night, the Rocky Marciano photograph on the wall.
The Bethnal Green caff with the marquetry walls, Pellicci family breakfasts since 1900.
The art-deco Westminster caff of 1946, full English at the formica tables.
Afternoon tea at the Piccadilly grocer's since 1707.
The Wimpy Bar, Britain's first hamburger chain, from Lyons' Coventry Street Corner House in 1954.
The grandest pub in England: marble, mosaic and the famous gents', across from the Phil.
The Rice Street pub where John Lennon drank as an art student.
Lime Street's great hotel of 1914, the Sefton Suite and the French restaurant.
Corned beef hash and a pint in the Victorian chop house on Cross Street since 1867.
The Edwardian railway hotel where Rolls met Royce in 1904; tea in the Octagon.
The coffee-house chain of the North and Wales, a Saturday afternoon in town in the 1950s and 60s.
The Harrogate and York tea rooms since 1919: fat rascals and Yorkshire tea from the trolley.
The Guiseley fish and chip palace with chandeliers, opened in 1928.
The longest bar in the city, in Drury Street since 1884.
Ice cream and fish teas in the Byres Road booths since 1918.
Oysters under the Doulton tiles of the Victorian bar off Princes Street, since 1863.
Birmingham's oldest pub, timber-framed in Digbeth since 1368.
The great Victorian gin palace of Aston, tiles and snob screens, since 1901.
Coffee roasters in the Grainger Market since 1750.

properties.description: The narrow Victorian pub on Side with the stained glass and the gramophone.
The Park Place Italian of 1983, a Cardiff night out under the photos of the famous.
The Victorian market hall of 1891: Welsh cakes from the stall, cockles and laverbread.
The gaslit Victorian gin palace on Great Victoria Street, snugs and stained glass since 1885.
The Grafton Street café of 1927, Harry Clarke windows and sticky buns.
Ireland's oldest pub, on Bridge Street since 1198.
The bascule bridge of 1894, raised for the tall ships.
The Serpentine, Speakers' Corner, and the Stones' free concert of 1969.
Nelson, the lions, the pigeons and New Year's Eve in the fountains.
Eros and the neon signs, the centre of the West End.
The Changing of the Guard and the balcony on the great days.
The twin towers, the 1966 World Cup final, and the FA Cup every May until 2000.
The Argyll Street variety theatre, Sunday Night at the London Palladium and the Royal Variety.
The dance hall of 1919, big bands and the Saturday night foxtrot; closed in 2007.
The great oval of 1871: the Proms, the boxing and the Beatles in 1963.
The Swinging London street of boutiques, 1966 on every corner.
The Festival of Britain pleasure gardens of 1951 and their funfair, and the peace pagoda.
The Palm House and the pagoda, a Sunday out by the river.
The Mathew Street cellar where the Beatles played nearly three hundred times between 1961 and 1963.
The Three Graces and the Mersey ferry.
The barber, the bank and the shelter in the middle of the roundabout.
The Kop in full voice, Shankly's Liverpool.
The Palm House and the boating lake in the great Victorian park.
The zoo, the speedway, the circus and the Bobs roller coaster in Gorton, 1836 to 1987.
The Theatre of Dreams, Busby's Babes and the 1968 European Cup side.

properties.description: Waterhouse's Gothic palace of 1877 on Albert Square.
The Hallé's home, and where someone shouted 'Judas' at Bob Dylan in 1966.
The city's biggest park, the tram museum and the boating lake.
The Holte End and the claret and blue.
The 1964 shopping centre and the market that was there long before.
The boating lake, the bandstand and the Midlands Arts Centre.
The weekend market in the East End, 'the Barras', and the Barrowland Ballroom above it.
The red sandstone palace of 1901, the organ recital at one o'clock.
The Hampden Roar, Scotland against England and the 1960 European Cup final.
The castle on the rock, the One o'Clock Gun and the Tattoo every August.
The floral clock, the bandstand and the castle above.
Edinburgh's seaside: the promenade, the open-air pool of 1936 and the funfair.
The lakes and the Tropical World, one of the biggest city parks in Europe.
The great Victorian market hall of 1857, where Marks & Spencer started as a penny bazaar.
Revie's Leeds United of the sixties and seventies.
The green arch of 1928 over the river between Newcastle and Gateshead.

properties.description: The Magpies' ground above the city since 1892.

properties.description: The home of Welsh rugby, the anthem before kick-off, until the Millennium Stadium.
The Norman keep and Burges's Victorian fantasy rooms in the middle of the city.
The lake, the lighthouse clock tower and the rowing boats.
The Edwardian baroque dome over Donegall Square.
The 1862 concert hall on Bedford Street; the Mulholland organ and everyone from Dickens to Led Zeppelin.
The Palm House and the Tropical Ravine beside Queen's University.
The Victorian park in the middle of the city, the ducks and the bandstand.
The home of Gaelic games: the All-Ireland finals every September.
The GPO, Clerys clock and Nelson's Pillar until 1966.
The Tower, the Golden Mile, the Illuminations and the Pleasure Beach.
The Palace Pier, the Lanes, the pebbles and the bank holiday mods and rockers.
The two bays, the Grand Hotel and the open-air theatre.
Windermere steamers, Beatrix Potter's Hill Top and the fells.
Fishing villages, cream teas, the long drive down the A30.
The ferry from Portsmouth, Shanklin Chine and the 1970 festival.
The first Butlin's holiday camp of 1936: the Redcoats, the chalets and the knobbly knees contest.
Dreamland, the Lido and the sands at the end of the Kent line.
The longest pleasure pier in the world and the Kursaal.
The English Riviera, palm trees on the seafront.
The castle, the Royal Mile, the Festival and the Tattoo.
The bonnie banks, half an hour from Glasgow, the steamer Maid of the Loch.
Doon the watter: the Clyde steamer to Bute for the Glasgow Fair.
The Victorian promenade between the Great and Little Orme, the pier and Punch and Judy.
Whitmore Bay and the funfair, the valleys' day at the seaside.
The mountain railway to the top of Snowdon and the slate villages.
Barry's Amusements, the strands and the Giant's Causeway down the coast.
The promenade and Bray Head, the DART and the Sunday out from Dublin.
The lakes, the jaunting cars and the Ring of Kerry.
Catalonia's rocky coast of coves and fishing villages, the package-holiday dream of the 1960s.
The first fortnight abroad: high-rise hotels, the Levante beach and the Spanish sun.
Palma, Magaluf and the first charter flights of the sixties.

properties.short_description: 'Freight Train' (1957) with Nancy Whiskey: a Soho coffee-bar skiffle group at the 2i's.
'Don't You Rock Me Daddy-O' (1957): the Soho band that came out of the 2i's Coffee Bar.
'Last Train to San Fernando' (1957): a Tennessee-born skiffle singer who worked in London with the Blue Grass Boys.
'Singing the Blues' (1957): Britain's first rock-and-roll star, discovered in a Soho skiffle cellar.
'Freight Train' (1957): the Glasgow voice of Britain's skiffle boom.
Leader of The Vipers, later a broadcaster of country and folk on the radio.
